options: A dynamic management view showing SQL Server's actual, current lock state — every lock currently granted or waiting
A stored procedure that releases all locks on a table
A table that permanently logs every lock ever taken, historically
A setting that enables or disables locking server-wide
questions.explain: It is a real-time DMV: querying it shows the lock state at that exact moment, system-wide.

questions.q: What does the request_mode column show?
options: Which lock type is held or wanted — S, X, U, IS, IX, SIX, Sch-S, Sch-M
The name of the database being queried
How many rows the query returned
The isolation level of the session
questions.explain: request_mode matches exactly the lock types covered throughout this chapter.

questions.q: What is the difference between request_status = 'GRANT' and request_status = 'WAIT'?
options: GRANT means the lock is actually held; WAIT means the session is blocked waiting for it
GRANT means the session has permission to connect; WAIT means it is disconnected
They mean the same thing — both indicate a held lock
GRANT only applies to shared locks, WAIT only applies to exclusive locks
questions.explain: A WAIT row is exactly how you spot a session that is currently blocked behind someone else's lock.

questions.q: Which column lets you trace a specific lock back to the session holding or waiting for it?
options: request_session_id
resource_database_id
resource_type
request_mode
questions.explain: request_session_id is the SPID, letting you connect a row in this view to an actual session and its running query.

questions.q: In the worked example, what does Session B's row in sys.dm_tran_locks show while it is blocked?
options: request_mode = 'S' with request_status = 'WAIT'
request_mode = 'X' with request_status = 'GRANT'
request_mode = 'Sch-M' with request_status = 'GRANT'
No row appears at all for a blocked session
questions.explain: Session B's plain SELECT is requesting a shared lock and is blocked, so it shows S / WAIT until Session A's transaction ends.
